subject: art-design
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which type of clay is fired at the highest temperature and typically becomes vitrified and slightly translucent?
questions.explain: Porcelain is fired at very high temperatures, producing a dense, vitrified and often translucent body.

questions.q: What is the name of the first firing of clay that hardens it before glazing?
questions.explain: The bisque or biscuit firing hardens the clay into a porous state ready to receive glaze.

questions.q: Why is an armature used when modelling a figure in clay or plaster?
options: To add colour to the surface
To provide an internal support structure
To speed up the firing process
To create a glossy glaze finish
questions.explain: An armature is an internal framework that supports soft modelling material and stops it collapsing.

questions.q: A pot built by rolling clay into long ropes and stacking them is made using which technique?
questions.explain: Coiling builds a vessel by layering and joining rolled ropes of clay.

questions.q: Shaping clay on a rotating potter's wheel is known as what?
questions.explain: Throwing is the process of forming clay on a spinning potter's wheel.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a subtractive making process?
options: Material is added and built up in layers
Material is removed to reveal a form
Molten material is poured into a mould
Sheets are folded and joined together
questions.explain: Subtractive processes such as carving work by cutting away material from a solid block.

questions.q: A simple pot formed by pressing a thumb into a ball of clay and squeezing the walls is called a what?
questions.explain: A pinch pot is shaped by pressing a thumb into a clay ball and pinching the walls outwards.

questions.q: In three-dimensional design, what does the term 'negative space' refer to?
options: The solid mass of the object
The empty space around and within a form
The base or plinth of a sculpture
questions.explain: Negative space is the empty area surrounding and passing through a form, which shapes how it is read.

questions.q: A sculpture designed to be viewed from all sides is described as which of the following?
questions.explain: Freestanding, or 'in the round', sculpture is fully three-dimensional and viewable from every angle.

questions.q: A sculpture in which forms project from a flat background surface is known as what?
questions.explain: Relief sculpture has forms that project from, but remain attached to, a flat backing plane.

questions.q: What is a key difference between a thermoplastic and a thermosetting plastic?
options: A thermoplastic can be reheated and reshaped, a thermosetting plastic cannot
A thermosetting plastic can be reheated and reshaped, a thermoplastic cannot
Both can be reheated an unlimited number of times
Neither can be shaped when heated
questions.explain: Thermoplastics soften and can be remoulded on reheating, whereas thermosetting plastics set permanently.

questions.q: What is the name for liquid clay used for casting and for joining clay pieces?
questions.explain: Slip is clay mixed with water to a liquid consistency, used for casting and joining.

questions.q: Slab building is a construction technique that involves which of the following?
options: Rolling clay into flat sheets and joining them
Pouring molten metal into a mould
questions.explain: Slab building uses rolled flat sheets of clay cut and joined to form a structure.

questions.q: A designer needs to produce many identical metal components from a single master. Which process is most suitable?
questions.explain: Casting molten metal into a reusable mould reliably reproduces identical components.

questions.q: To join two pieces of leather-hard clay securely, what should you do?
options: Score both surfaces and apply slip
questions.explain: Scoring and applying slip creates a strong bond that will not crack apart during drying and firing.

questions.q: In a three-dimensional structure, what is a cantilever?
options: A projecting element supported only at one end
A curved arch spanning two columns
questions.explain: A cantilever is a beam or form fixed at one end that projects into space unsupported at the other.

questions.q: In three-dimensional design, what is a maquette?
options: A small preliminary or scale model
questions.explain: A maquette is a small-scale model made to develop and test ideas before creating the final piece.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of an additive making process?
options: Building up a form by modelling clay
questions.explain: Additive processes create form by adding and building up material, as in modelling and construction.

questions.q: A student wants to permanently fuse two steel bars together using intense heat. Which process should they use?
questions.explain: Welding uses high heat to melt and fuse metal edges into a single joined piece.

questions.q: In three-dimensional design, what does 'proportion' describe?
options: The relationship in size between parts and the whole
The weight of the finished object
questions.explain: Proportion concerns how the sizes of individual parts relate to each other and to the whole form.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Art & Design (1AD0) specification; Three-Dimensional Design
